opus-5.5.text:
Well, the fundamental difference is that text is discrete. In a language model you have a finite vocabulary, maybe 30,000 to 100,000 tokens, so when the system predicts the next token it can't know exactly which word comes next, but it can produce a probability distribution over all the possible words. That's easy: a big vector of numbers between zero and one that sum to one. Handling uncertainty in that discrete space is straightforward.

The real world isn't like that. If you take a video and ask a system to predict what happens next at the pixel level, there are an essentially infinite number of plausible continuations. We don't know how to represent a probability distribution over all possible video frames in a high-dimensional continuous space in any tractable way. When you train a system to predict pixels, it can't commit to one future, so it hedges and produces a blurry average of all the possibilities, which is useless. People have been trying this for 15 or 20 years, and it basically doesn't work.

There's also the issue that much of the world is inherently unpredictable at the level of detail. If I film this room and pan the camera, the system cannot predict the texture of the carpet or the exact position of every leaf on a tree outside the window. It shouldn't even try. Spending capacity predicting those details is a waste.

That's why I've been advocating joint embedding predictive architectures, JEPA. Instead of predicting the input itself, you encode both the observation and the future into an abstract representation space and make predictions there. The encoder can learn to discard details that aren't predictable and keep what is: where objects are, how they move, what the consequences of an action will be. That's much closer to what humans and animals do. We don't predict the world pixel by pixel; we predict at an abstract level.

And the amount of data matters too. A four-year-old child has taken in through vision roughly as much data as the biggest LLMs are trained on in text. Most of what we know about the world, intuitive physics, object permanence, cause and effect, comes from that sensory experience, not from language. So if we want machines that understand the physical world, can plan, and can reason, scaling next-token prediction on text won't get us there. We need systems that learn world models from sensory input, and that requires a different architecture.

r001.rationale: It says language models predict over a finite vocabulary of discrete tokens, making uncertainty tractable as a probability distribution over possible words.

r002.rationale: It says JEPA encodes the observation and future into an abstract representation space and makes predictions there.

r003.rationale: It does not describe the trivial constant-representation solution where every input receives the same representation.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the world is not a sequence of discrete symbols drawn from a finite vocabulary. Text is easy in a very specific sense: the space of possible next tokens is finite, something like a hundred thousand possibilities, and so you can represent your uncertainty about what comes next as a probability distribution over that set. You just produce a big softmax, train with cross-entropy, and it works beautifully. That's really the trick that makes LLMs tractable.

Now look at the physical world. The inputs are continuous, high-dimensional, and noisy. If I ask you to predict the next frame of a video, or where this coffee cup will be in half a second, the space of plausible futures is not a list you can enumerate. It's a continuum, and most of the details in it are fundamentally unpredictable. You cannot predict the exact pattern of leaves on a tree in the wind, the exact texture of a wall as the camera moves, the precise way a sleeve wrinkles. There are an enormous number of futures that are all equally compatible with what you've seen.

So if you naively apply the LLM recipe, meaning predict the raw pixels and minimize some reconstruction error, two things go wrong. First, representing a distribution over a high-dimensional continuous space is intractable. You can't normalize it. Second, if you train the system to make a single prediction, it averages over all the possible futures and produces a blurry mess, because the mean of several plausible futures is not itself a plausible future. We saw this for years with video prediction. Every architecture produced blur.

What I've argued for, and what the JEPA line of work is about, is that the system should not predict in pixel space at all. It should learn an abstract representation of the world and make predictions in that representation space, where it's allowed to discard all the details that are inherently unpredictable or irrelevant. The representation of the tree shouldn't encode every leaf. The question becomes not "what will the pixels be" but "what are the properties of the next state that I can actually anticipate," and then you predict those.

And there's one more difference I think is underappreciated. Language is a very low-bandwidth, already highly abstracted signal. Humans did the hard work of compressing the world into words. An LLM learns from the product of human perception and reasoning. A system that has to learn from video and sensory data is doing the compression itself, from scratch, and that's precisely the hard part, the part that a four-year-old does effortlessly and that no current AI system does well. So I don't think the autoregressive token prediction paradigm is wrong for text. I think it's the wrong tool for understanding the physical world, and understanding the physical world is what you need for planning, for reasoning about consequences, for what you'd actually call common sense.

r001.rationale: The response says the next-token space is finite and discrete (about a hundred thousand possibilities), making uncertainty representable as a distribution over those tokens.

r002.rationale: It argues that real-world prediction should happen in a learned abstract representation space rather than pixel space.

r003.rationale: The response does not explain that predicting one input’s encoded representation from another’s permits a trivial constant-representation solution.

astra-6.text:
Well, the main difference is that the real world is not a sequence of discrete symbols. With language, you have a finite vocabulary, and you can train a system to produce a probability distribution over the next token. The world is continuous, high-dimensional, and only partially observable. There are many things you cannot predict precisely.

Imagine a camera looking at a street with trees. You might be able to predict that a car will continue moving along the road, but you cannot predict the exact position of every leaf. If you train a system to predict every pixel of the next video frame, you are asking it to spend an enormous amount of effort on details that don't matter.

So the question is: can we predict in a representation space that captures the important aspects of the world and leaves out the unpredictable details? You want to know what objects are present, how they move, and how your actions will affect them. You don't necessarily need to generate an image of all of that.

That's the kind of world model I'm interested in. It allows a system to anticipate the consequences of actions and use those predictions to plan. Next-token prediction can capture a lot of knowledge about the world, but learning to continue text and learning how the world evolves under your actions are different objectives.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the world with language’s finite vocabulary and says the model can produce a probability distribution over the next token, presenting that discrete space as the basis for next-token prediction.

r002.rationale: It says world prediction should happen in a representation space that captures important aspects while leaving out unpredictable details.

r003.rationale: It does not describe predicting one input’s encoded representation from another or the trivial constant-representation solution.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the real world is only partially observable, and a lot of what happens is unpredictable. If you look at a video of a room and try to predict every pixel a second from now, you have to predict things like the exact motion of leaves outside the window. That’s both extremely difficult and largely irrelevant to understanding what’s happening in the room.

Language has already discarded an enormous amount of that detail. It’s a discrete, compressed description of reality. Predicting the next token is certainly a useful learning task, but predicting how the world evolves requires deciding what information to retain and what uncertainty to ignore.

So the approach I favor is to predict in an abstract representation space. You encode what you observe, and you predict the representation of a future observation, rather than all its pixels. Ideally, that representation captures things like objects, their interactions, and the consequences of actions, without requiring you to predict every detail.

Then you can use that world model to plan: if I take this action, what is likely to happen? That’s the capability we want—not simply generating a plausible description, but anticipating consequences well enough to choose what to do.

r001.rationale: The response calls language discrete and compressed, but does not attribute next-token prediction’s tractability to a finite space of possible tokens.

r002.rationale: It explicitly favors predicting a future observation’s encoded representation in an abstract representation space.

r003.rationale: It does not mention the trivial constant-representation solution when predicting one input’s representation from another.
